meta.title: Who really said "If You Want to Know What a Man's Like, Look at How He Treats His Inferiors"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. K. Rowling did write it — for Sirius Black in Goblet of Fire (2000), p. 525. But the thought was in newspapers by 1910 and in a letter of 1748.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If You Want to Know What a Man's Like, Look at How He Treats His Inferiors'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Rowling: Sirius Black's line in Goblet of Fire (2000), verified at p. 525. The idea itself dates back well over a century further.

answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence is dialogue Rowling wrote for Sirius Black in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2000), and Quote Investigator verified it on paper ↗ at page 525 of the Scholastic first American edition. The full line runs longer than the version that usually circulates: “If you want to know what a man’s like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals.”

source.excerpt: If you want to know what a man’s like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the passage and cites it to Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, page 525, Arthur A. Levine Books / Scholastic Press, New York, 2000 — marked “Verified on paper.”
Wikiquote ↗ independently lists the line under Sirius Black with the same page 525 reference, on a page describing the novel as written by J. K. Rowling and first published in 2000.
The exchange sits in chapter 27, “Padfoot Returns” ↗, where Sirius, hiding in a cave near Hogsmeade, discusses Crouch and the sacking of the house-elf Winky.

The same QI investigation establishes what the line is not: original. Its closest documented forerunner is a passage by Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken printed in the Mansfield News of Ohio on 29 January 1910 ↗, with the theme traceable to a Chesterfield letter of 1748.
source.excerptNote: Quoted in brief for identification. In the scene, Harry, Ron and Hermione visit Sirius in a cave outside Hogsmeade; Hermione is angry that Barty Crouch Sr. dismissed his house-elf Winky, Ron tells her to let it go, and Sirius sides with Hermione — telling Ron she has the measure of Crouch better than he does before delivering the line.

author.name: J. K. Rowling
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 1965 · British novelist · author of the Harry Potter series
author.bio: Joanne Rowling was born on 31 July 1965 in Yate, Gloucestershire, and is best known for the seven-volume Harry Potter series, which began with Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone in June 1997. Goblet of Fire, the fourth book, arrived on 8 July 2000 — the first in the series published in Britain and America on the same day. The house-elf storyline that produces this line is one of the series’ running arguments about servitude and how the powerful behave when nobody is watching.

Rowling, Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Scholastic, 2000), p. 525. The thought is much older: a close version appeared in print in 1910, credited to Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The credit to Rowling is correct — unusually, for a name this heavily targeted by fake quotes. What goes wrong is everything around it: the wording drifts, the originality is overstated, and reworded versions surface under other famous names.

items.why: Shared as though Rowling coined the insight. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes she did not originate the saying, and documents close analogues in 1911, 1910, 1902, 1852, 1805 and a Chesterfield letter of 17 May 1748.

Loosely reworded versions circulate under her name — for example “If you want to see the true measure of a man, watch how he treats his inferiors, not his equals,” credited to Rowling on quote sites ↗. The book’s sentence begins “If you want to know what a man’s like, take a good look at…”

“Judge a man not by how he treats his equals but by how he treats his inferiors” travels under Chaplin’s name on aggregator sites — Goodreads carries it with no source work ↗, on a page that notes its quotes are community-added and unverified. It is neither the Goblet of Fire wording nor tied to any documented Chaplin text.

items.who: Rowling speaking in her own person
items.why: The sentence is written for a character. In the scene summarised in chapter 27, “Padfoot Returns” ↗, Sirius Black says it about Barty Crouch Sr. after Crouch dismissed his house-elf — not an authorial aphorism but a judgement one character passes on another.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Rowling’s sentence, spoken by Sirius Black in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2000) and verified on paper at page 525 ↗ — but a very old idea in a new suit.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: The line comes out of the series’ longest-running moral argument: how wizards treat house-elves. Hermione is furious that Barty Crouch Sr. dismissed his elf, Winky; Ron tells her to drop it; Sirius takes Hermione’s side and says the way Crouch handles the people beneath him is the tell. It is a character judgement delivered inside a plot, which is part of why it travels so well — it arrives as advice rather than as a theme.

But the thought is far older than Hogwarts. Quote Investigator ↗ traces close relatives back through a 1911 remark by Dr. M. C. B. Mason, an 1910 newspaper passage from Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken, an 1852 Farmer’s Cabinet article titled “Courtesy to Inferiors,” an 1805 definition of a gentleman, and a Lord Chesterfield letter of 17 May 1748. Rowling gave an old maxim its most quotable modern sentence.
context.detailsSummary: The pre-Harry-Potter paper trail, as documented by Quote Investigator
detailsBody: 1748 — Lord Chesterfield, in a letter to his son dated 17 May, writes that the mark of a well-bred man is to converse with his inferiors without insolence.
1805 — William Parnell’s enquiry into discontent in Ireland defines a gentleman as one who treats his inferiors, whatever their station, with civility and affability.
1852 — The Farmer’s Cabinet of Amherst, New Hampshire runs “Courtesy to Inferiors,” arguing a man’s claim to refinement is best tested by how he treats his inferiors in life.
1910 — Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken’s line, printed in the Mansfield News of Ohio on 29 January and reprinted widely, is the closest documented match before Rowling.
2000 — Sirius Black’s version appears in Goblet of Fire, and becomes the phrasing the internet remembers.
context.pull: It is the way one treats his inferiors more than the way he treats his equals which reveals one’s real character. — Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken, 1910

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator transcribes the exact line "If you want to know what a man's like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals" as spoken by Sirius Black to Ron Weasley, cites Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2000), Page 525, Arthur A. Levine Books: Imprint of Scholastic Press, New York, marked 'Verified on paper', concludes Rowling did not originate the saying, and documents precursors in 1748 (Chesterfield letter of 17 May 1748), 1805 (William Parnell), 1852 (Farmer's Cabinet, 'Courtesy to Inferiors', Amherst NH), 1902 (Printers' Ink), 1910 (Rev. Charles Bayard Miliken, Mansfield News, Ohio, 29 January 1910), 1911 (Dr. M. C. B. Mason), 1913 and 1930.
Wikiquote's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire page lists the line under Sirius Black with the reference 'Pg 525', and describes the work as written by J.K. Rowling and first published in 2000.

The Muggles' Guide chapter 27 page ('Padfoot Returns') quotes the line and places it in the cave scene where Sirius discusses Bartemius Crouch, and describes Hermione's comment about Crouch firing his house-elf Winky.

Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire was first published on 8 July 2000 by Bloomsbury (UK) and Scholastic (US), the first book in the series published in both countries simultaneously; author J. K. Rowling.

Joanne Rowling was born 31 July 1965 in Yate, Gloucestershire; she is a British author best known for the seven-volume Harry Potter series, which began with Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone on 26 June 1997.

Goodreads displays the full wording 'If you want to know what a man's like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals.' attributed to J.K. Rowling, Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.

A reworded variant, 'Judge a man not by how he treats his equals but by how he treats his inferiors,' is attributed to Charlie Chaplin with no source work cited, on a page noting that quotes are community-added and not verified by Goodreads.
A drifted wording, 'If you want to see the true measure of a man, watch how he treats his inferiors, not his equals,' is published credited to J.K. Rowling.

Quote Investigator's companion article on the related saying 'You can easily judge the character of a man by how he treats those who can do nothing for him' credits Malcolm Forbes based on current evidence (earliest cite Earl Wilson's 1972 column), and finds the Goethe and Samuel Johnson attributions unsupported.
